headline: For once oil and bonds are both up: Houthi strikes on Saudi Aramco sites lifted Brent ≈2.7% to ≈$111–112, yet the 10Y fell to ≈5.07–5.09%. An AI-earnings selloff (Lam −6–8%, Tesla capex cut, Meta's $9.9B charge) knocked Nasdaq futures down ≈1.3–1.8% and sent money into Treasuries ahead of 7:30 claims and the noon $26B 5Y TIPS sale.
summary: Risk-off pre-market (Bloomberg/Benzinga, ≈6:00 AM CT): S&P futures ≈−0.7% to −1.0%, Nasdaq-100 ≈−1.3% to −1.8% (erasing most of its 2.2% weekly gain), Dow ≈−0.5%. Wednesday closed S&P 7,757.17 (+0.58%) and Dow 52,856.09 (+0.69%). Lam Research is ≈−6–8% despite $8.22B revenue vs ≈$8.13B, on a wide guide, December shipments slipping into March and lower China sales. IBM beat on revenue ($17.1B vs $16.82B) but fell; TI beat ($2.62 vs $2.42 EPS) and was ≈flat.

Musk/Meta: Tesla earned $0.48 adj. vs ≈$0.45 on ≈$28.05B revenue with FCF of +$1.53B, but cut 2026 capex to ≈$20B and pushed out Optimus/robotaxi timelines. Shares reversed from $386.47 to ≈$374 after hours. Meta revenue rose 26% to $64.6B (vs ≈$63.3B) with a $73–76B Q4 guide, but GAAP EPS was $3.83 after a $9.9B legal charge. Q3 capex was $34.9B, FY range narrowed to $135–145B, FCF ≈−$2.1B, and it plans a new non-voting Class C stock. Shares +2.5–5% after hours, but the stock is now ≈−1% pre-market.

Oil vs. rates: Houthi strikes on an Aramco field and an Eastern Province airport (≥3 killed; a drone aimed at Shaybah was intercepted) pushed Brent to ≈$111.6–112.3 (+$2.8), near a 5-month high. The U.S. ordered non-emergency staff out of Saudi Arabia. Treasuries rallied anyway: T-notes +16 ticks and the 10Y ≈5.07–5.09% (range 5.08–5.16%, Newsquawk), vs Wednesday's ≈5.11%. Equity risk-off and haven demand are outweighing the inflation hit from oil this morning. The DXY is ≈101.6 (−0.2%), and the yen and franc lead G10.

Fed: still in blackout before Oct 27–28. FedWatch shows ≈83–84% hold / ≈16% hike for October. December hike odds read 76–90% depending on the snapshot. A Reuters poll has 94 of 100 economists expecting a hold next week and all 100 expecting a December hike. Today's claims (7:30 CT, ≈200K vs 199K) are the last labor print before the meeting. A jump would be the first data to dent December pricing.

Supply and real yields: Treasury sells a $26B new 5Y TIPS at noon CT. Pre-auction talk puts the real yield ≈2.55–2.60%, vs a ≈2.37% 5Y breakeven (nominal 5Y ≈4.89%, Tipswatch). Wednesday's 20Y reopening tailed ≈0.9 bp at 5.469%. A soft TIPS sale with oil at $111 would show inflation protection is expensive while real-rate buyers are still demanding a concession.

Metals and Chicago: gold fell ≈$54 to ≈$4,086 (Kitco 6:17 ET, range $4,066–4,145), even though yields and the dollar both slipped, which looks like liquidation rather than a rates story. LME copper closed Wednesday at $14,370.5 (−0.59%) as LME stocks rose 8% in a week. In Chicago, Abbott will spin off its $8.5B Nutrition unit (Similac, Ensure) tax-free by end-2027, and CME says open interest topped 133M contracts after a record Q3.
markets_asof: Close 3:00 PM CT (metals ≈1:45 PM CT; yields late session)

calendar.event: Earnings: Lockheed (out), Blackstone (out), Union Pacific (6:45 AM), Honeywell, American Airlines, P&G, Valero
calendar.prior: Actual: LMT $7.97 adj., rev $20.7B, FY EPS guide $30.35–30.75, backlog $292B · BX GAAP NI to BX $662M, div $1.12 (Q2 $1.29)
calendar.why: American is the cleanest read on what $111 Brent does to airline margins after United's weak guide (AAL EPS estimates are down 58% in 60 days). Blackstone's dividend cut from $1.29 to $1.12 signals slower realizations, a read-through for capital-markets fees.
This is the last labor data before the Oct 27–28 FOMC. A clear upside surprise is the only thing on today's calendar that could cut into the ≈80–90% December hike pricing and steepen 2s10s.
This is a secondary print. A fresh decline would add to the housing-led growth-scare story (record-low pending sales, 7.5% mortgages).

calendar.event: Chicago Fed Survey of Economic Conditions (Oct)
calendar.why: It is the Midwest read on activity and hiring plans, and the Chicago Fed's own data, so useful for local networking conversations.
Regional surveys are showing input-price pressure from diesel and energy. A hot prices-paid reading supports the hawks.
With a ≈2.37% breakeven and oil at $111, this tests demand for inflation protection. A tail of 3+ bp would push real yields toward ≈2.70% and pressure gold.
Friday's flash PMIs and next week's PCE are the last inputs. Reuters' poll is unanimous for a December hike.

rates.title: Bonds rally even as oil spikes, because fear beats inflation this morning
rates.body: T-notes gained 16 ticks overnight and the 10Y traded 5.08–5.16% before settling ≈5.07–5.09%, roughly 3–4 bp below Wednesday's ≈5.11%, even with Brent +$2.8 to ≈$111–112 (Newsquawk; Bloomberg via PANews). The catalysts were the AI-earnings selloff and the U.S. ordering non-emergency staff out of Saudi Arabia. The 30Y hit a 1-week low of 5.397%.
rates.simple: Usually higher oil pushes bond yields (the interest rate a bond pays) up, because it means more inflation. This morning investors are more scared of a stock drop and a wider Gulf war, so they are buying the safest asset, U.S. government bonds, which pushes yields down. If this lasts, mortgage rates could ease a little, but it rests on fear, not on good news about inflation.

rates.title: Fed: October hold is near-certain; December hike is the consensus trade
rates.body: FedWatch puts an Oct 28 hold at ≈83–84% (hike ≈16%), and December hike odds range from 76% to ≈90% depending on the snapshot. A Reuters poll shows 94 of 100 economists expecting a hold next week and all 100 a December hike. The effective fed funds rate is 3.88% (H.15).
rates.simple: The Fed sets a target for the overnight rate banks charge each other. Traders bet on its next move using futures (contracts that pay off based on where rates end up). Markets are almost sure the Fed waits next week but raises rates in December to fight 3.7% inflation. That keeps loan, credit-card and deposit rates high into 2027.

rates.title: Noon test: $26B 5Y TIPS with real yields ≈2.6% and breakevens only ≈2.37%
rates.body: The new 5Y TIPS (settles Oct 30) is expected near a 2.55–2.60% real yield. The 5Y breakeven is ≈2.37% against a 4.89% nominal 5Y (Tipswatch), and April's new issue cleared at 1.367%. The coupon is set 1/8 point below the auction yield.
rates.simple: TIPS are Treasury bonds whose principal rises with inflation. Their 'real yield' is what you earn on top of inflation. The 'breakeven' (the gap between normal and inflation-protected yields) is the inflation rate the market expects, and at ≈2.4% it is well below today's 3.7% CPI. That means investors trust the Fed to bring inflation down. A weak auction would push real yields higher, which tightens financial conditions and usually hurts gold.

rates.title: Global: JGBs and haven FX catch the bid; ECB hawks stay vocal
rates.body: Japan's 10Y closed at 2.88%, a 6-week low, and the yen and franc are the top G10 performers on haven flows, while NZD fell on cooler CPI. An ECB member said more tightening may be needed if inflation stays above target. Euro Stoxx 50 futures are −0.6% after Wednesday's +1.5% to 6,213.
rates.simple: When investors get nervous, they buy currencies and bonds seen as safe, such as the Japanese yen, the Swiss franc and government debt. Japan's 10-year yield near 2.9% is very high by its own history. That matters because Japanese investors are big buyers of U.S. bonds and may keep more money at home.

derivatives.title: CME: Treasury futures OI +1.2M contracts to 24M; September ADV a record 7.7M
derivatives.body: CME's October Rates Recap shows Treasury futures open interest up 1.2M contracts (≈$75M DV01) to ≈24M, and September Treasury futures ADV of 7.7M was the highest September ever, beating the prior high by nearly 2M/day. Treasury futures-plus-options OI set its all-time record of 36.33M in February.
derivatives.simple: Open interest is the number of futures contracts still open, a measure of how many positions people are holding. DV01 is how much money those positions gain or lose per 0.01% move in rates. Rising open interest at 5% yields means more investors are hedging or betting on rates, which earns fees for CME and is the business rates desks run.

derivatives.title: CME's Q3 call: open interest above 133M and Q4 ADV tracking +17%
derivatives.body: Total OI ended Q3 at 128M contracts, a record for an end-September, and topped 133M by the call date. Management flagged that weekly and short-dated expirations distort year-on-year OI comparisons. Q4 ADV is tracking +17% vs last year's record Q4, after Q3 ADV of 29.4M (+16%).
derivatives.simple: CME runs the futures exchanges where banks, funds and companies hedge rates, oil, metals and stocks. Trading is booming because rates, oil and geopolitics are all volatile, and that shows up directly in CME's record revenue. The caveat: more very short-term options trading inflates some of the headline numbers.

derivatives.title: Earnings vol: the AI complex reprices and option markets brace for big single-stock moves
derivatives.body: Nasdaq-100 futures are ≈−1.3% to −1.8% after Lam (≈−6–8%), IBM and Tesla (≈−3% after hours) disappointed, and Meta's capex range rose to $135–145B with FCF ≈−$2.1B. Options imply an ≈8% move in Spotify on today's report. Single-stock event risk is driving index vol this week, not macro.
derivatives.simple: Options are contracts that pay off if a stock moves past a set price. Their prices show how big a move traders expect, called implied volatility. This week, results from a few giant tech and AI companies are moving the whole market, so traders are paying up to protect against sharp swings in individual names.

metals.title: Gold drops ≈$54 to ≈$4,086 even with lower yields and a softer dollar
metals.body: Kitco had spot gold at $4,086.00 bid at 6:17 ET (−$54.30, −1.31%), with a $4,066–4,145 range, after Wednesday's late ≈$4,141. That puts it back near the ≈$4,076 support level flagged this week. Both the 10Y (≈−3 bp) and DXY (−0.18%) are lower, so the usual drivers don't explain the drop. This looks like liquidation alongside the equity selloff and fully priced December hike odds.
metals.simple: Gold usually rises when interest rates and the dollar fall, because it pays no interest and is priced in dollars. Today it is falling anyway, which often happens when investors sell what they can to cover losses elsewhere. If the stock selloff deepens, gold can fall at first and recover later.

metals.title: Copper: LME stocks up 8% in a week, Codelco's record premium and an 'AI is overhyped' debate at LME Week
metals.body: LME 3M copper closed Wednesday at $14,370.5/t (−0.59%), ≈3.4% below the Sept 10 record of $14,875. LME stocks rose 11,475 t in a day and 8% in a week, while Codelco is offering a record $350/t premium over LME. A Fastmarkets/Bloomberg LME Week panel called AI an 'overhyped' demand driver. Strike risk at Highland Valley Copper is a new supply wildcard.
metals.simple: Copper goes into wiring, power grids and data centers, so its price tracks the global economy. More copper sitting in exchange warehouses means less tightness right now. But the world's biggest producer charging a record premium for future supply shows buyers still expect shortages, so the long-term story still points up.

metals.title: Silver and PGMs drift: silver ≈$57.4–57.7, platinum ≈$1,624–1,641
metals.body: Wednesday quotes put silver at $57.36–57.67, platinum at $1,624–1,641 and palladium at ≈$1,076–1,087 (Fortune 8 AM ET; Metalcharts). No reliable Thursday print was found, but silver usually trades as high-beta gold, so expect it lower with today's ≈1.3% gold drop.
metals.simple: Silver and platinum are both precious and industrial metals: they're used in jewelry and investment, and also in solar panels, electronics and car exhaust systems. That double role makes them swing more than gold. When gold falls and growth worries rise, as now, they tend to fall harder.

banking.title: Blackstone cuts its quarterly dividend to $1.12 from $1.29
banking.body: Blackstone's Q3 release (8-K, this morning) shows GAAP net income ≈$1.3B ($662M attributable to BX; $2.5B YTD). The dividend falls to $1.12/share from Q2's $1.29, when distributable earnings were $2B ($1.52/sh). Q3 distributable earnings weren't in the material I could access.
banking.simple: Blackstone is the world's biggest private-equity and real-estate investor. It pays shareholders based on profits from selling investments. A smaller dividend suggests fewer or less profitable exits this quarter, which matters to banks because those sales generate M&A, IPO and loan-refinancing fees.

banking.title: Meta's capex machine: $34.9B a quarter, negative FCF and a new non-voting share class
banking.body: Meta guided 2026 capex to $135–145B and raised FY expenses to $175–179B (including a $9.9B legal charge). Q3 FCF was ≈−$2.12B, and it announced a non-voting Class C stock. With hyperscaler capex now outrunning operating cash flow, expect more jumbo IG bond deals and new equity structures, a growing fee pool for DCM/ECM desks.
banking.simple: Meta is spending more on AI data centers than its business brings in, so it will probably have to borrow or raise money from investors. The new non-voting shares let it sell stock without diluting Mark Zuckerberg's control. For investment banks, that means big bond and stock deals to underwrite (help sell to investors).

banking.title: Regional bank M&A keeps grinding: Peoples–Capital, Trailmark approval, TowneBank–blueharbor
banking.body: Peoples Bancorp's pending deal for Capital Bancorp creates a ≈$14B-asset franchise. Adams Community and Pittsfield Cooperative won FDIC/Massachusetts approval Oct 21 to form Trailmark Bank, and TowneBank is buying blueharbor for ≈$154M (Q1 2027 close). Big 2026 closes so far: Santander/Webster $12.3B, Fifth Third/Comerica $10.9B, Pinnacle/Synovus $8.6B.
banking.simple: Banks merge to get bigger and spread the cost of technology and regulation across more customers. Regulators are approving deals faster this year, so mid-sized banks are combining steadily. That reshapes who lends to local businesses and creates advisory work for bank-focused investment bankers.
banking.source: Harvard Law Forum on Corporate Governance / Investing.com

banking.title: Union Pacific reports at 6:45 AM CT with the $85B Norfolk Southern deal still at the STB
banking.body: Consensus is ≈$3.47 EPS on $7.14B revenue. The STB accepted the revised merger application effective May 28 but held it in abeyance pending supplemental filings. A final decision may not come until ≈Sept 2027, and the companies target a 2027 close.
banking.simple: Union Pacific wants to buy Norfolk Southern to create the first coast-to-coast U.S. freight railroad. A federal board (the STB) has to approve it, and shippers and rival railroads are fighting it as anticompetitive. It is one of the biggest pending M&A deals, and banks are financing and advising on it.

banking.title: IPO pipeline: Lycia Therapeutics' $250M Nasdaq deal is set for this week
banking.body: Lycia set terms for a $250M IPO at $16–18/share. Calendars disagree on whether it trades Oct 22 or Oct 23. It tests biotech risk appetite on a day the Nasdaq is set to open ≈1.5% lower.
banking.simple: An IPO (initial public offering) is when a private company first sells shares to the public, with banks underwriting the deal. Selling-day market mood matters a lot. If stocks are falling, companies may price at the low end or delay, which cuts banks' fees.

cnbc.title: Futures sell off as Meta and Tesla lead the AI trade lower; oil rises
cnbc.body: CNBC's live blog frames the morning as an AI-earnings reversal: mega-caps Meta and Tesla slid after their reports while oil jumped on Gulf tensions. Bloomberg's tally has Nasdaq-100 futures −1.7% and S&P −1%.
cnbc.simple: Stocks of the biggest tech companies are falling before the open because investors question whether all the money spent on AI will pay off. Higher oil prices from Middle East attacks add to the gloom, since they raise costs for businesses and consumers.

cnbc.title: Treasury yields steady as investors await jobless claims
cnbc.body: Wednesday's close: the 2Y rose <1 bp to 4.791% and the 30Y fell >1 bp to 5.41%, with the 10Y ≈5.11%. The 20Y reopening drew 2.73x cover at 5.469%. Claims are seen at ≈200K vs 199K.
cnbc.simple: Bond yields (the interest the government pays to borrow) barely moved Wednesday as traders waited for new jobs data. Weekly unemployment claims are a fast gauge of layoffs. A big jump would hint the economy is cooling and could make the Fed less eager to raise rates.

cnbc.title: Tesla beats but cuts capex; shares reverse lower after hours
cnbc.body: Tesla posted $0.48 adj. EPS vs ≈$0.45 on ≈$28.05B revenue, with auto gross margin ex-credits of 18.1% (from 16.3%) and FCF of +$1.53B. Operating income fell 56% y/y and 2026 capex was cut to ≈$20B. Shares fell from a $386.47 close to ≈$374 after hours.
cnbc.simple: Tesla made more profit per car than expected and generated cash instead of burning it, but investors focused on the delays to its robot and self-driving taxi plans. Since much of Tesla's stock price rests on those future bets, pushing them back hurt more than the good quarter helped.

wsj.title: Musk personally ordered the Starlink slowdown that hit Ukraine's drones
wsj.body: The Journal reports, citing U.S. officials, that Musk ordered a speed cap on the military-grade Starlink service Ukraine depends on, and later discussed it with President Trump. It lands as SpaceX and Tesla boards form merger committees for a combination valued at ≈$3.5T.
wsj.simple: Starlink is SpaceX's satellite internet, and Ukraine's army relies on it to fly drones. If one person can throttle a military's communications, governments and investors will question how risky it is to depend on Musk's companies, and that could matter for SpaceX contracts and the Tesla merger review.

wsj.title: Meta leads the Journal's front: bigger AI spend, a legal hit and a new share class
wsj.body: Reuters' WSJ digest leads with Meta. Revenue beat at $64.6B, but a $9.9B legal charge cut GAAP EPS to $3.83, FY expenses rose to $175–179B, and Meta will create non-voting Class C shares.
wsj.simple: Meta earned more from ads than expected, but it is spending heavily on AI and took a large legal charge. The new class of shares without voting rights lets it raise money while the founder keeps control. Some investors see that as poor governance.

wsj.title: Tesla aims to sell Cybercab robotaxis by year-end despite a federal probe
wsj.body: The Journal's coverage alongside the Meta lead says Tesla still targets Cybercab sales by year-end even as federal safety investigators examine its self-driving tech. The earnings call pushed out wider robotaxi and Optimus timelines.
wsj.simple: Tesla wants to sell a self-driving car with no steering wheel. Regulators are looking into whether its driver-assist software is safe, and that could slow approvals. The gap between Tesla's promises and what it delivers is now the main debate for its stock.

tribune.title: Abbott will spin off its $8.5B Nutrition business by end-2027
tribune.body: The Abbott Park–based company will distribute the Nutrition unit (Similac, Ensure, Pedialyte, Glucerna; ≈16,000 staff, 14 plants) tax-free to shareholders, led by Daniel Salvadori. RemainCo keeps devices, diagnostics and established pharma (≈$42B sales). 2026 guidance is unchanged and the CEO ruled out a sale. Shares slipped.
tribune.simple: A spin-off gives existing shareholders shares in a new, separate company instead of selling the business. Abbott wants to wall off its baby-formula unit, which has been hit by recalls and lawsuits, so the rest of the company can be valued as a medical-device maker. For banks, this means advisory work and probably a new debt package for the spun-off company.

tribune.title: CME Group's record quarter: open interest past 133M, Q4 volume tracking +17%
tribune.body: After a record Q3 (revenue $1.737B, adj. EPS $3.02 vs $2.98, ADV 29.4M), management said OI rose from 128M at quarter-end to >133M and Q4 ADV is running +17% vs a record Q4 2025.
tribune.simple: CME, based in Chicago, earns a small fee on every futures and options trade. Volatile interest rates, oil and metals mean more hedging and more trades, so CME is one of the few companies that benefits directly from market turmoil.

tribune.title: Chicago Fed: regional survey out today; national activity index was −0.04 in August
tribune.body: The Chicago Fed releases its Survey of Economic Conditions today. The CFNAI was −0.04 in August (from 0.08 in July), just below the trend-growth line of zero, and the September CFNAI is due Oct 26, two days before the FOMC decision.
tribune.simple: The Chicago Fed National Activity Index combines 85 economic indicators into one number, where zero means the economy is growing at its normal pace. A slightly negative reading means growth is a bit below trend. That is the kind of slowdown the Fed is weighing against high inflation.

nyt.title: Labor market is 'solid but stagnant'
nyt.body: The Times' Oct 21 business section argues hiring has stalled without mass layoffs. Claims near 199K and slow payroll growth fit that picture, which is why today's claims print matters for December Fed pricing.
nyt.simple: Companies aren't firing many people, but they aren't hiring much either. People who have jobs are fairly safe, but job seekers have a hard time. For the Fed, that makes a rate hike less risky for jobs but still a gamble.

nyt.title: $8 billion aid plan to cover farm losses from diesel costs
nyt.body: The administration announced an $8B plan to offset farmers' losses from soaring diesel prices, a direct fiscal cost of the $100+ oil shock.
nyt.simple: Farmers run tractors and trucks on diesel, and oil near $110 has driven fuel costs sharply higher. The government is spending money to cushion them. That adds to federal borrowing at a time when the Treasury already pays above 5% on long-term debt.

nyt.title: New lawsuit challenges Canada tariffs; Boeing's 737 Max wins a U.S. approval
nyt.body: A suit challenges the president's authority to impose tariffs on Canada. Separately, Boeing won a U.S. approval tied to the 737 Max. Amazon plans 300,000 seasonal hires.
nyt.simple: Tariffs are taxes on imports, and courts may limit how freely the president can impose them. That matters for prices and trade-sensitive companies. Boeing's approval helps it deliver more planes, and Amazon's large seasonal hiring suggests retailers expect a decent holiday season.

talking_points.topic: Oil up, yields down: which channel wins?
talking_points.point: This morning Brent rose ≈$2.8 while the 10Y fell ≈3 bp, so the haven/growth channel beat the inflation channel. The tell will be breakevens. If the 5Y breakeven (≈2.37%) rises while the 10Y falls, the real-yield component is collapsing, which helps duration and eventually gold. If the noon TIPS auction tails, the market is still demanding real-rate compensation even with 3.7% CPI and a December hike ≈fully priced.

talking_points.topic: Exchange volume is the cleanest volatility trade
talking_points.point: Treasury futures OI rose 1.2M contracts (≈$75M DV01) to 24M, September Treasury ADV was a record 7.7M, and CME OI is above 133M with Q4 ADV tracking +17%. A sharp interview question: how much of that is basis-trade and hedge-fund leverage that could unwind quickly, and how does the growth in short-dated options change risk at the clearinghouse?

talking_points.topic: Copper: tariff arbitrage vs. physical tightness
talking_points.point: LME copper is ≈3.4% below its $14,875 record as LME stocks rose 8% in a week, yet Codelco is asking a record $350/t premium over LME and Highland Valley strike risk is rising. On a metals desk, the trade is the spread structure, not the outright price: near-term surplus versus forward tightness, plus the COMEX–LME arbitrage driven by the threat of a U.S. refined-copper tariff.

caveats: WSJ, NYT and Tribune are paywalled, and direct page fetches were blocked this run, so stories come from search excerpts: the Reuters WSJ press digest (MarketScreener), the NYT print-edition index (PressReader), Crain's and Bloomberg excerpts for Chicago, and other outlets' coverage. Pre-market yields, futures and Brent are ranges because sources and timestamps differ. No Thursday prints were found for the Russell 2000, WTI, silver or copper, so those tiles carry Wednesday levels or '—'. Blackstone's distributable EPS and the December hike odds (76–90%) could not be pinned down.

updates.label: Close
updates.headline: Tech had its worst day since June (Nasdaq −2.6%) and the 10Y closed under 5% (≈4.99%, −12.5 bp, its biggest one-day drop since Aug 2025), while gold (≈−2.5%) and silver (≈−5.5%) kept selling off even with lower yields and $112 Brent.
points: Close: S&P 500 7,663.43 (−1.21%), Nasdaq Comp 26,008.86 (−2.6%; Reuters has −2.7%), Dow 52,867.98 (+0.02%), per CNBC. Chips led the drop: AMD −8%+, Micron −6%, Nvidia −4%, Meta ≈−7%. The Dow finishing flat is the rotation the brief flagged. I couldn't find a Russell close.

Rates: Benzinga's late-session print has the 10Y at ≈4.99% (−12.5 bp) and the 2Y at ≈4.69% (−11.9 bp), so 2s10s is ≈+30 bp, about where it started the day. This was a parallel haven rally and not a Fed repricing: December hike odds are still in the high 80s. Correction to the brief: the 5.07–5.09% 10Y level is stale by ≈8–10 bp.

$26B 5Y TIPS (new issue): high real yield 2.367% vs 2.360% when-issued, so a 0.7 bp tail. Bid-to-cover 2.41, the weakest since Apr 2025 (6-auction avg 2.52). Indirects took 62.1%, directs 32.4%, dealers 5.5%. The coupon is 2.25%, and the real yield is the highest at auction for this tenor in ≈3 years. It came in well below the ≈2.52–2.60% pre-auction talk because nominals rallied, which implies a 5Y breakeven around ≈2.3–2.4%.

Metals: Kitco at 2:46 PM ET had gold at ≈$4,033 (−$107, −2.6%) and silver at ≈$54.64 (−5.6%), breaking FXStreet's ≈$54.77 support and setting a new 2026 low. Copper ≈$6.34–6.36/lb (≈−2.5–2.8%). The pattern of gold falling while yields fall and oil rises suggests liquidation and Fed-hike fears, not a real-yield story.

Oil and tomorrow: Brent traded as high as $113.40, its highest since May 5, and WTI ≈$100 (+3%) after the State Department ordered non-emergency staff out of Saudi Arabia. I hadn't seen official settles when this was written (Wed: Brent $108.82, WTI $97.15). Friday: S&P Global flash PMIs at 8:45 AM CT (mfg cons. 55.5 vs 55.9 prior, services 57.9 vs 58.8, per TD) and final UMich sentiment at 9:00 AM CT. These are the last inputs before the Oct 27–28 FOMC blackout ends.
updates.simple: Investors sold big tech companies, worried they're spending too much on AI, and put the money into U.S. government bonds. That buying pushed the 10-year yield (the interest the government pays to borrow for 10 years, which mortgage rates follow) to its biggest one-day drop in over a year. The government also sold inflation-protected bonds (TIPS, whose payout rises with inflation). Buyers demanded slightly more than expected, so the sale went fine but not great. Gold and silver fell hard anyway: traders still expect the Fed to raise rates to fight oil-driven inflation, and higher rates make metals that pay no interest less attractive.

updates.label: Midday
updates.headline: The risk-off move got bigger by noon. The 10Y fell below 5% (≈4.996%, −15 bp) for the first time since Sept 23, the Nasdaq is down ≈2.1%, and gold and silver are still falling even as yields drop.
points: Rates: CNBC has the 10Y at ≈4.996% (−15 bp), its first trade below 5% since Sept 23. That is ≈4 bp lower than at the post-open update (≈5.03%). The drivers: a run out of AI stocks after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's comments on capital scarcity, plus the NYT report that the U.S. and Israel are weighing new Iran strikes. A Substack roundup citing CME FedWatch has December hike odds at ≈88%, so this rally is a haven bid and not a repricing of the Fed. Midday 2Y and 30Y prints weren't available.

Equities at noon ET (247wallst): S&P −1.22% (≈7,662), Nasdaq Comp −2.15% (≈26,120), Dow −0.26% (≈52,720). Semis are reversing Wednesday's gains. updates.simple: Investors are selling tech stocks and buying the safest asset there is, U.S. government bonds. Heavy demand for bonds pushes their yield (the interest rate the government pays to borrow) down, and the 10-year yield, which mortgage rates follow, fell below 5% for the first time in a month. Gold usually rises when yields fall. It is falling today because traders still expect the Fed to raise rates in December to fight oil-driven inflation, and higher rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.

points: Claims: 194K initial vs ≈200K consensus (prior revised up to 200K), a 3-month low; 4-wk avg 197,750. Continuing claims rose 25K to 1.728M, a 6-week high. Layoffs stay low but rehiring is slow, so this doesn't dent the 89–90% December-hike pricing.

Rates: the 10Y is ≈5.03% (−11 bp) and the 30Y ≈5.35% (−8 bp), per CNBC. The 2Y was ≈4.73% before the print. updates.simple: Each week the government counts new unemployment claims (people who just lost a job and applied for benefits). Fewer people filed than expected, which means companies aren't laying off. Normally that would push interest rates up. Instead, bond yields (the interest rate the government pays to borrow) fell sharply. Investors were scared by a tech-stock selloff and new Middle East war risk, so they bought safe Treasuries. Higher oil is also starting to hurt companies like airlines, which spend heavily on fuel.
